newsitem.title: UK: Weather at fore as Europe grain exports near close.
newsitem.headline: Weather at fore as Europe grain exports near close.

text.p: As the European grains export campaign nears a close, weather is increasingly dominating traders' thinking.
But problems elsewhere in the world, rather than the excitement caused by a lack of rain in western Europe were the main fundamental issue, they said.

"The important thing now is the weather in the U.S. and Canada," one European exporter told Reuters in midweek. "Drought in the UK and France shouldn't matter much yet," he said. "but come back in May or June and tell me there's still drought and I'll get worried."
There was some worrying damage to Spanish crops, he conceded. Spain's drought was broken Thursday by heavy rain.
European wheat exports have pretty well played themselves out, the German trader said. His impression was confirmed by the EU's decision Thursday to halt its weekly wheat tender.
Barley exporting will go on for a bit longer, "but not much," he said.
In France, worsening water shortages lifted prices, though gains looked slippery by Friday.
And a last-minute scramble before the EU barred the door to most new export licences for last year's crop boosted April and May deliveries two percent to 925-930 francs.
"We have done enough," an EU official said, noting that exports had risen more than 60 percent since the previous year.
Another said the rise in prices was directly responsible for the decision to clamp down on exports several weeks earlier than usual and now it was up to the market to respond.
"The priority is our domestic market again. If we are being restrictive with exports, it's not because of world prices, it's because of the extremly firm interior prices," he said.
He said the decision should force cooperatives suspected of holding back supplies to reflect again.
The EU has also left a deliberate cloud over its export policy for the next harvest, hoping to stamp out what it regards as excessive speculation on a drought.
"We will be prudent before starting to export again," he said, adding that weather would be the main factor.

Traders and analysts say weeks without rain in the big grain regions is starting to hit potential yields. But it will be at least another 10 days before the problem starts to become irreversible and another month after that before there is serious damage, a government crop analyst said.

Analysts said France produced a record 1996 crop despite identical drought fears 11 months ago, after a break in the weather. But two years of accumulated damage to sub-soil water levels had left a lower margin for recovery than last year.
German wheat traders saw local markets underpinned by lack of sellers and speculative interest from international export trade houses.
This would offset the price dampening effect of the EU's move, they said.
"Brussels managers have assured the local industries of supply security and appeased the watchful U.S. but I don't see prices dropping over the next two to three weeks," one said.
Local milling wheat demand was muted but buyers were seen interested in prices around five marks below current levels.
Feed grain markets were also quiet as buyers were holding out for lower levels, pointing to lower than expected offers into intervention.
Cool weather had not spoiled prospects for a good 1997 grain harvest in Germany.
UK traders expected firm prices to stay. "As long as there's drought in the UK and France, we will maintain a steady note," one said, although he noted a forecast of possible rain in early May.
A firm Chicago market was also a bullish factor, although he pointed out that Chicago's most recent rise was inspired by EU export policy. "It's a bit of a circle," he said.
The French market is also helping to keep the UK market well supported, another trader said.

Traders still complained about a lack of volume off farms. And they reported good recent export demand to Spain and Portugal, assisted by the dry weather in those countries. "And you don't need an (EU) export licence to do that," one said.
In Spain, prices rose due a tight supply both in foreign markets, especially in the UK and France, and at home.
Dealers said heavy rain nationwide on Thursday night, and forecast of further rainfall suggested easing in prices in the coming week and good buying conditions.
Italian wheat prices continued their upward trend this week on diminishing supplies as the new crop season approaches. Prices of imported wheat rose, and demand from feed producers increased.

"Feed producers have been resorting to wheat lately because there is a fungus on maize which could be poisonous for animals. This, which makes maize unusable, and the fact that flour prices have risen, has forced producers to resort to wheat," one dealer said.
Dealers said there has been some fear over the recent dry weather, especially in Northern Italy, but also in some major production areas of the South.
But they said it was still difficult to forecast how much this drought will influence the next harvest and the maize and sunflower sowings which are due to start in the next few weeks.
